Do not introduce deadlines or policies beyond what is provided there. ::: ## Meet your instructor {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="20%"} ::: ::: {.column width="80%"} - Varada Kolhatkar [[ʋəɾəda kɔːlɦəʈkər](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Phonetic_Alphabet)] - You can call me Varada, **V**, or **Ada**. - Associate Professor of Teaching in the Department of Computer Science. - Ph.D. in Computational Linguistics at the University of Toronto. - I primarily teach machine learning courses in the [Master of Data Science (MDS) program](https://masterdatascience.ubc.ca/). - Contact information - Email: kvarada@cs.ubc.ca - Office: ICCS 237 ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Introduce yourself and how students can address you. Briefly connect your computational linguistics background to your interest in learning patterns from data. Point out the contact information and invite questions during class. Transition: "I'd also like to hear where you're starting from." ::: ## Activity 1 {.slide-your-turn} \ Discuss the following questions with your neighbour. - Where have you encountered machine learning? - What's one thing you're excited or unsure about? ::: {.notes} Give neighbours about one minute to discuss both prompts. Invite two or three brief responses, including one uncertainty if someone is willing to share. Use their examples as connections later in the lecture. They do not need to know the terminology yet; this is a chance to surface experience and questions. ::: ## Today’s big questions {.slide-goals} - What is machine learning, and when is it useful? - How do we represent a prediction problem with features and a target? - How do baselines and decision trees learn and make predictions? - How do we evaluate predictions and control tree complexity? ::: {.notes} Describe the arc: understand learning from examples, organize a prediction problem, build a simple reference model, and improve it with a decision tree. Emphasize that students will both read a model and use code to fit it. Today we measure training performance; whether the model works on unseen examples is the question for Lecture 2. ::: # AI, ML, and DL ::: {.notes} Transition from students' everyday examples to the vocabulary. "These terms are often used together. Let's distinguish them, then make learning from examples concrete." ::: ## Where do AI, ML, and DL fit? {.slide-your-turn} Quick discussion: which of these might use AI, machine learning, or deep learning? - A spam detector 📧 - A basic calculator ➕ - A chatbot planning your holiday 💬 ::: {.notes} Use this as a quick verbal discussion, about 30–60 seconds. Ask for reasoning rather than a single definitive label. A spam detector could use explicit rules or a learned model. A basic calculator is ordinary computation. A modern holiday chatbot may use a deep learning language model alongside tools such as a calculator or search. The task name alone does not tell us how the system is built. Transition: "The next diagram describes the relationship between the approaches." ::: ## What are AI, ML, and DL? ![](img/ai-ml-dl.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" height="400px"} Our focus: learning from examples and applying what we learn to new cases. ::: {.notes} Point from the outer category inward. AI is the broad field of building systems with capabilities such as perception, reasoning, and planning. ML is an approach that learns patterns from data or experience. DL is a type of ML using neural networks with many layers to learn representations and predictions. Not all AI learns from data: search and rule-based systems are examples of other approaches. Keep this distinction brief; students do not need a history of AI here. Our focus is learning from examples and using what we learn on new cases. Transition: "What does learning a pattern actually look like?" ::: ## Image classification {.smaller} Searching photos for animals involves **image classification**. Imagine telling cats and foxes apart. How might we do this with traditional programming? With ML? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="35%"} ![](img/cat-or-fox.png) ::: ::: {.column width="65%"} | Image ID | Whiskers Present | Face Shape | Fur Colour | Label | |----------|------------------|------------|------------|-------| | 1 | Yes | Round | Mixed | Cat | | 2 | Yes | Round | Brown | Cat | | 3 | Yes | Pointed | Red | Fox | | 4 | Yes | Pointed | Red | Fox | | 5 | Yes | Round | Grey | Cat | ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Ask students what clues they would use to tell a cat from a fox. Then connect their suggestions to the table: a row is one example, the descriptive columns are features, and Cat/Fox is the known label. Image ID identifies the row; it is not an animal characteristic. Ask: "Which column helps distinguish the labels in this small table? Which doesn't?" Face shape and fur colour distinguish these examples; whiskers are always present and do not separate them. These are illustrative, manually supplied features, not a reliable biological rule. Transition: "Who decides how to combine those clues into a prediction?" ::: ## Who writes the rules? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} **Traditional programming** We write the rules. **Pointed face + red fur** ↓ Predict **fox** ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} **Machine learning** We provide labeled examples. **Features + cat/fox labels** $\to$ Learn a **prediction rule** ::: :::: ::: {.fragment} **What would happen with either approach if we encountered a fox with white fur?** ::: ::: {.notes} Read the two workflows side by side. With explicit programming, we specify the prediction rule. With supervised ML, we supply examples and labels, and a learning algorithm fits a rule. ML can learn rules too; the difference is where the rule comes from. Before revealing the white-fox question, ask students what could go wrong with the hand-written rule. A white fox fails the red-fur condition. A learned model might also fail if it relies on colour; it might succeed if it uses face shape. We cannot know without inspecting or testing it. Both approaches need evaluation on new cases. Transition: "For images, deep learning can also learn useful representations instead of requiring us to describe every feature." ::: ## DL approach: example :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](img/cat-or-fox.png) ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} - A neural network automatically learns which features to look at (edges $\rightarrow$ textures $\rightarrow$ objects). - No need to even specify face shape or fur colour. It learns relevant features on its own. ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Contrast the input representations: the previous example supplied face shape and fur colour; an image network can start with pixel values and learn intermediate representations during training. Edges, textures, and objects are an intuition for increasingly complex representations, not a guaranteed sequence for every network. For this supervised cat/fox task, we still supply training labels. Learning representations does not remove the need for suitable data, design choices, and evaluation. We will focus on tabular supervised learning rather than training image networks in this course. ::: ## Ways of learning from data {.smaller visibility="hidden"} - **Supervised learning:** predict targets from labeled examples - **Unsupervised learning:** discover structure without supplied targets - **Reinforcement learning:** learn actions through interaction and rewards - **Generative AI:** generate content; models can use several learning approaches - **Recommendation systems:** learn preferences, often combining multiple approaches These categories are not mutually exclusive. ::: {.notes} Optional orientation only; this slide is hidden in the main presentation. Supervised learning uses known targets, unsupervised learning looks for structure without designated targets, and reinforcement learning uses interaction and rewards. Generative AI describes generating content, and recommendation describes an application; these are not additional mutually exclusive learning approaches. Return to supervised learning as the course focus rather than expanding the taxonomy. ::: ## Supervised learning: inputs, targets, and predictions {.smaller} - **Inputs ($X$):** observations described by features, such as fur colour and face shape. - **Targets ($y$):** labels or values we want to predict, such as cat or fox. - **Training:** learn a model $f$ relating inputs to targets. - **Prediction:** use the model to predict targets for unseen examples. ![](img/sup-learning.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" height="280px"} ::: {.notes} Use cats and foxes to name each part: X contains the descriptive features, y contains the known animal labels, and training produces a model f. Trace the diagram in two stages: labeled examples produce a fitted model; the fitted model then receives the features of a new example and returns a prediction. The new label is not supplied when predicting. Ask: "What would we need later to check whether that prediction was right?" Its actual label. Transition: "Before building a model, should this problem use ML at all?" ::: # When should we use ML? ::: {.notes} Frame this as choosing an appropriate starting point for a problem. Having an ML tool available does not make it the best tool for every task. ::: ## ❓❓ Rules, ML, or human judgment? {.smaller .slide-your-turn} Choose a starting point for each problem and explain why. Combinations are possible. - **(A)** Checking whether an email address ends with `@student.ubc.ca` - **(B)** Predicting which songs a listener might enjoy - **(C)** Awarding a scholarship based on a student's personal essay Where could mistakes cause harm, and who should be responsible? ::: {.notes} Give students about one minute to choose starting points and explain why. If using a single iClicker vote, ask which starting point they would choose for song recommendations, stating the response options aloud; discuss the other two examples verbally. Suggested answers: A uses an explicit suffix check; B can use ML to learn preferences from examples; C requires accountable human judgment about criteria and context. ML might assist with C, but a predicted score does not settle who deserves an award. Debrief orally: rules fit known, precise logic; ML fits useful patterns in representative data when rules are hard to write and errors can be evaluated; human judgment matters when values, empathy, context, and accountability are central. Systems can combine all three. Ask briefly where errors would cause harm. Close with: "Making a prediction does not automatically justify handing the decision to a model." ::: ## Rules, ML, or human judgment? {.smaller visibility="hidden"} | Starting point | When it is appropriate | |---|---| | **Explicit rules** | The logic is known, stable, and can be stated precisely. | | **Machine learning** | Useful patterns exist in representative data, hand-written rules are difficult, and we can evaluate errors. | | **Human judgment** | Context, empathy, values, or accountability are central to the decision. | Real systems can combine all three. Making a prediction does not automatically justify delegating the decision to a model. ::: {.notes} Hidden reference slide: the oral debrief on the preceding activity carries this content. If showing the table for clarification, summarize each row with the email, song, and scholarship examples. Emphasize representative data and the ability to evaluate errors as conditions for using ML. The three starting points can be combined; human oversight does not by itself guarantee a good outcome. ::: # Formulate a prediction problem ::: {.notes} Transition: "We've seen how examples can teach a model to distinguish animals. Now we'll build a small model ourselves using a table of job attributes." ::: ## Which job might make you happy? {.slide-your-turn} You've graduated and have several job offers. **Which one would make you happiest?** ![](img/happy-vs-sad-employee.png){.nostretch fig-align="center" width="400px" fig-alt="Happy vs sad employees"}
Image created by GPT-6 Astra
- **What job attributes would you record?** - **What outcome would you predict, and how would you represent it?** ::: {.notes} Invite two or three suggestions for job attributes, then ask what outcome students would record. Imagine looking for patterns in the experiences of friends with similar priorities. Possible targets are Happy/Unhappy or a numerical satisfaction score. Clarify what each measures; encoding Happy as 1 does not turn classification into regression. This is an invented teaching dataset, not evidence about what causes happiness. A prediction could inform someone's job choice, but does not make that choice for them. Transition: "Let's inspect the examples we have." ::: ## Toy job happiness dataset ::: {#3ac147ca .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Explain that 0/1 encodes no/yes for the binary attributes; salary is a numerical amount. There are seven examples, small enough to inspect together. boss_vegan is an arbitrary candidate feature, not a claim about diet and happiness. A recorded feature is not automatically useful or causal. Ask students to identify features, target, and one example. X consists of supportive_colleagues, salary, free_coffee, and boss_vegan. y is happy?. Each row is one person in a job. The displayed subset has three rows, while the full dataset has n = 7 examples and d = 4 features. Features must be available when making the prediction. The unknown happiness answer cannot also be an input. ::: ## Training vs. Prediction - Training: learn the mapping - Known features $X$ + known targets $y$ $\to$ fitted model $f$ - Prediction: use the mapping - New features $X_{\text{new}}$ $\to$ fitted model $f$ $\to$ predictions $\hat{y}_{\text{new}}$ **We need known targets to train the model, not to make predictions.** ::: {.notes} Walk through the job example twice. During training, we have job attributes and known happiness labels. During prediction, we provide attributes to the already fitted model and receive its proposed happiness label. Explain that y is a known target and y-hat is a prediction. Prediction does not itself refit the model, and a prediction may differ from the eventual observed label. Known targets are needed to train this supervised model and to evaluate predictions, but not to produce predictions. The goal is useful performance on new examples. ::: ## Same job features, different targets {.smaller} ::: {#71905d37 .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Supportive
colleagues		 Salary ($) Free
coffee		 Boss
vegan		 Happy? happiness_score
0 70,000 0 1 Unhappy 35
1 60,000 0 0 Unhappy 48
1 80,000 1 0 Happy 85
``` ::: ::: - **Happy or unhappy** $\to$ predict a discrete label $\to$ **classification** - **Happiness score from 0 to 100** $\to$ predict a numerical quantity $\to$ **regression** Other regression examples: predicting temperature, house price, or travel time. ::: {.notes} Keep the job attributes fixed and change the question we ask. Happy/Unhappy asks for a category: classification. A satisfaction score asks for a numerical quantity: regression. The happiness scores are invented for illustration. In this table, happy? and happiness_score are alternative outcomes; happy? should not be included as a feature when illustrating prediction of an unknown happiness score. A numerical encoding of categories is still classification. Transition: "Let's classify a few prediction tasks by the kind of answer they require." ::: ## iClicker 1.1: Classification or regression? {.slide-your-turn} **Select all regression problems.** - **A.** Predict whether a flight will be delayed. - **B.** Predict a flight's delay in minutes - **C.** Predict a student's percentage grade in DSCI 571. - **D.** Predict whether you'll get a seat on the bus. - **E.** Predict whether you'll hit snooze tomorrow morning. ::: {.notes} Give students 30–60 seconds before discussing responses. Correct answers: B and C are regression because the targets are delay in minutes and percentage grade. A, D, and E ask for yes/no categories, so they are classification. Compare A with B: the same flight context can support either task depending on the target. If C is confusing, distinguish predicting a percentage from predicting a letter-grade category. Classification versus regression depends on the meaning of the target, not simply how it is stored. ::: # Train, predict, and evaluate models using `scikit-learn` ::: {.notes} Transition from identifying the data's roles to implementing them. "We'll start with a deliberately simple model so that a more complicated model has something to beat." ::: ## Separate the inputs from the target ::: {#f605b160 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = toy_happiness_df.drop(columns=['happy?']) y = toy_happiness_df['happy?'] ``` ::: | Object | Contains | Shape | |---|---|---| | `X` | Four feature values for each person | `(7, 4)` | | `y` | One known happiness label per person | `(7,)` | **Keep the answer out of the inputs.** ::: {.notes} Read the two lines: drop happy? to construct the feature table; select happy? to construct the target Series. These operations organize the data, not train a model. Explain the shapes: X has seven rows and four columns; y has one label for each of the seven rows. Row alignment matters: each target must belong to the corresponding feature row. Keep the answer out of the inputs. Transition: "Before using these features, how well could we do by ignoring them?" ::: ## Your turn: predict without the features {.slide-your-turn} ![](img/happy_unhappy_faces.png){.nostretch width="320px" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Seven training labels: four Happy and three Unhappy"} If you must predict **the same label for everyone**, which label should you choose? How many predictions will be correct? ::: {.notes} Allow 30–45 seconds. Ask for both the single label and the number of correct predictions. Answer: choose Happy, which occurs four times; this gets four of seven right. Always choosing Unhappy would get three right. This is the most-frequent baseline. It uses the training labels to choose its constant prediction, but ignores the job attributes. ::: ## A baseline gets four out of seven right ::: {#ce5a4827 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Actual Baseline prediction Correct?
Unhappy Happy No
Unhappy Happy No
Happy Happy Yes
Happy Happy Yes
Happy Happy Yes
Happy Happy Yes
Unhappy Happy No
``` ::: ::: **Always predict Happy:** accuracy $= 4/7 \approx 57\%$\ **Classification error:** $3/7 \approx 43\% = 1 - \text{accuracy}$ ::: {.notes} Read one correct and one incorrect row rather than the full table. Accuracy is correct predictions divided by all predictions: 4/7, about 57%. Classification error is the fraction incorrect: 3/7, about 43%. This is the performance of a constant prediction on our training examples. It is a reference point, not evidence that we learned useful relationships with job attributes. Transition: "Let's fit this same baseline using the interface we'll also use for decision trees." ::: ## Fit a baseline with scikit-learn We’ll use [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/), a Python machine learning library. ::: {#4ab8014b .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent') dummy.fit(X, y); ``` ::: **`fit(X, y)`** learns from the training data. Here, it finds the most frequent target. **This baseline ignores the feature values.** ::: {.notes} Introduce scikit-learn as the Python library we will use. Explain the sequence: import the estimator class, create an estimator with a chosen strategy, then fit it using X and y. Here fit learns which target is most frequent. DummyClassifier accepts X for a consistent interface even though this strategy ignores the feature values. Pause to distinguish creating the model object from fitting it. Transition: "Once fitted, we can request predictions and compare them with known answers." ::: ## Predict, then check accuracy ::: {#b057c210 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} dummy.predict(X) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` array(['Happy', 'Happy', 'Happy', 'Happy', 'Happy', 'Happy', 'Happy'], dtype='

Possible questions include whether colleagues are supportive or whether salary exceeds a threshold. Ask how the labels differ in the two resulting groups. A useful first question need not classify every example perfectly. Unlike the baseline, these questions use feature values. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} **Supportive colleagues** gives a cleaner split. ::: ::: {.notes} Pause before revealing the cleaner split. Supportive colleagues creates a no group with two Unhappy examples and a yes group with four Happy and one Unhappy. Boss vegan leaves both groups with mixed labels. Ask: "In which split are we more certain about the label within each group?" Supportive colleagues is better in this comparison. The Data tab is available if students want to check the counts. This comparison concerns the observed labels, not a causal explanation. It also does not prove this is the best question among all features; salary is another candidate. ::: ## How does a tree learn its questions? - Learn **which feature-based questions to ask, and in what order**. - At each node, compare candidate questions and choose a split that makes the groups' labels less mixed. - Repeat within each group, until a stopping condition is reached. - Each leaf predicts its most frequent training class. ::: {.notes} Connect the manual comparison to the algorithm: at a node, compare candidate feature questions, choose a split that reduces label mixture, and repeat within the resulting groups until a stopping condition is met. Leaves return their most frequent training label. These local choices do not guarantee the best possible whole tree. Gini impurity or entropy can quantify mixture; no formulas are needed today. Numeric features can be split using thresholds, such as salary <= 75000. Supportive colleagues beat boss_vegan in our comparison, but the algorithm also considers salary, so the fitted root may differ from our example. Optional reading: [Tree algorithms](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/tree.html#tree-algorithms-id3-c4-5-c5-0-and-cart). ::: ## Fit a decision tree ::: {#596c09de .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=1) model.fit(X, y); ``` ::: **Same `fit` interface. A different learning algorithm.** `max_depth=2` allows at most two questions along a prediction path. ::: {.notes} Compare these lines with the baseline code: import, construct, fit. The interface is the same; the learning algorithm changes. max_depth=2 permits at most two questions on a root-to-leaf prediction path. It does not mean two questions in the whole tree or guarantee that every path has length two. random_state makes this example reproducible. Leave the parameter/hyperparameter distinction until students have seen what was learned. Transition: "Let's read the questions that fitting produced." ::: ## Read the learned tree {.smaller} ::: {#a0ffddec .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-01-intro-terminology-decision-trees_files/figure-revealjs/cell-14-output-1.png){width=1192 height=607} ::: ::: **Root:** first question, **Branch:** answer to a question, **Leaf:** prediction ::: {.notes} Start at the root: salary <= 75,000. In this plot, True goes left and False goes right. Low salary predicts Unhappy; higher salary leads to the supportive_colleagues question. For a 0/1 feature, supportive_colleagues <= 0.5 means no supportive colleagues. Among the higher-salary examples, no supportive colleagues predicts Unhappy and supportive colleagues predicts Happy. Name root, branch, and leaf while pointing to them. value counts training labels in the order Happy, Unhappy; samples counts examples reaching the node. Leaf predictions use the majority label. Salary was selected first even though supportive colleagues beat boss_vegan in our earlier two-question comparison. Transition: "Now follow one new example through this tree." ::: ## Prediction {.model-plot .boundary-plot} What would be the prediction for the example below using this tree ? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {#6e83d0b3 .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-01-intro-terminology-decision-trees_files/figure-revealjs/cell-16-output-1.png){width=1192 height=607} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} - supportive_colleagues = 0 - salary = 100,000 - coffee_machine = 0 - vegan_boss = 1 ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Give students 30–45 seconds to trace the path before asking for an answer. Salary 100,000 fails salary <= 75,000, so go right. supportive_colleagues = 0 satisfies <= 0.5, so go left to Unhappy. Ask for the path as well as the label. Free coffee and boss diet are not used by this particular tree, even though they were supplied during fitting. The slide's coffee_machine and vegan_boss descriptions correspond to the dataset columns free_coffee and boss_vegan. The predicted label is not a known actual outcome. Transition: "The code should follow the same path." ::: ## Prediction with `sklearn` - supportive_colleagues = 0 - salary = 100,000 - coffee_machine = 0 - vegan_boss = 1 ::: {#90e8593f .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} test_example = [[0, 100000, 0, 1]] print("Model prediction: ", model.predict(test_example)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model prediction: ['Unhappy'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Ask students to predict the printed label before showing or reading the result: Unhappy. The nested list represents one example with four features, in the training-column order: supportive_colleagues, salary, free_coffee, boss_vegan. The outer list supplies the row dimension; scikit-learn expects a collection of examples, even for one prediction. Feature order and schema must match training. In practical code, a DataFrame with the training column names makes that correspondence clearer. We supply no happiness label. ::: ## Does the tree beat the baseline? ::: {#c550c5df .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.score(X, y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a32301f7 .cell execution_count=18} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Ask students what the phrase training accuracy adds before revealing the qualification. The tree fits these seven observed labels better. That does not show it predicts new people's happiness better or establish that its splits describe causes. Hold off on the full train/test procedure; Lecture 2 addresses the unanswered question. We supplied max_depth=2; fitting selected the salary and supportive-colleagues thresholds. Leaf predictions and the chosen split features are also learned. Reveal the depth definition and count the edges along the longest root-to-leaf path. A maximum depth is an upper limit, not a guarantee of exactly that depth. Hyperparameters can later be chosen using validation. Today, use depth to see how a constraint changes the model's questions and predictions. ::: ## Decision boundary with `max_depth=1` {.model-plot .boundary-plot .smaller} - **Points:** observed people and their actual labels - **Shaded regions:** the model's predicted class - **Decision boundary:** where the predicted class changes ::: {#53e1e875 .cell execution_count=19} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-01-intro-terminology-decision-trees_files/figure-revealjs/cell-20-output-1.png){width=2417 height=917} ::: ::: **Decision stump:** a depth-one tree. **Which person does it get wrong?** ::: {.fragment} The person earning **$150,000 without supportive colleagues**. ::: ::: {.notes} Orient students before discussing the error: the horizontal axis is supportive_colleagues (0 or 1), the vertical axis is salary, points show actual labels, and background regions show predicted labels. For this visualization, we fit a new model using only these two features. The binary horizontal feature has meaningful observed values at 0 and 1; the continuous background between them illustrates the model's regions. A depth-one tree asks only the salary question. Its boundary is at salary 75,000: lower salaries predict Unhappy and higher salaries predict Happy. A boundary marks where the predicted class changes, not a causal threshold. Pause before revealing the error: the person earning 150,000 without supportive colleagues is actually Unhappy but lies in the Happy region. Training accuracy is 6/7. Transition: "What happens if we allow one more question along the path?" ::: ## Decision boundary with `max_depth=2` {.model-plot .boundary-plot} Contrast it with the depth-two tree, which can ask another question within the higher-salary group. ::: {#60de44b8 .cell execution_count=20} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides-01-intro-terminology-decision-trees_files/figure-revealjs/cell-21-output-1.png){width=2417 height=917} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Keep the same axes and compare with the stump. The salary split remains; the higher-salary region receives an additional split on supportive colleagues. For higher salaries, only supportive colleagues = 1 predicts Happy. Trace the previously incorrect 150,000/no-supportive-colleagues example. It now falls in an Unhappy region, so all seven training examples are classified correctly. Relate the additional boundary to the additional tree question. Greater depth can make more detailed regions, but better training accuracy alone does not establish better predictions on new examples. ::: ## iClicker 1.3: Baselines and trees {.slide-your-turn} **Select all true statements.** - **A.** Changing salary values must change a most-frequent baseline's predictions. - **B.** `predict` needs features; `score` also needs known targets. - **C.** Decision-tree features must be binary. - **D.** A tree predicts by following a path from root to leaf. ::: {.notes} Correct answers: B and D. Give students time to choose, then request explanations for at least one false statement. A is false: changing salary alone, while keeping the same training labels, does not change a most-frequent baseline. B is true for these supervised estimators: prediction uses features and scoring also uses known targets. C is false: salary is numeric, and the tree learns a threshold. D is true: prediction follows questions from root to leaf.
